result: The study confirms that speed is underestimated when contrast is reduced uniformly (distance-independent reduction), replicating prior findings from classical vision research.
evaluation: Claims C3, C40, and C95 are well-supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 showing that uniform contrast reduction led to speed underestimation (PSE values of 95.5 and 95.2 km/hr matched to 65 km/hr clear visibility, equivalent to perceived speeds of 41.4 and 41.5 km/hr). This replicates established findings and serves as a validation control.

result: In distance-dependent contrast reduction (fog), speed is overestimated rather than underestimated, with participants matching lower actual speeds to clear visibility conditions.
evaluation: Claims C4, C37, C38, and C100 are strongly supported by Experiment 1 data showing that in fog conditions, participants matched lower speeds (54.7 and 41.7 km/hr) to clear visibility (65 km/hr), indicating speed overestimation (equivalent to 76.4 and 94.3 km/hr). Statistical significance (p<0.001) and effect sizes (ηG2 = 0.61) support this finding.

result: Speed overestimation in fog prompts drivers to decelerate, with participants driving significantly slower in fog conditions compared to clear visibility.
evaluation: Claims C5, C52, C55, C104, and C144 are supported by Experiment 2 behavioral data showing drivers drove slower in fog (77.3 and 70.9 km/hr) compared to clear visibility (85.1 km/hr), with statistical significance (p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.44). This demonstrates a direct link between perceptual overestimation and behavioral response.

result: Distance-independent (uniform) contrast reduction causes speed underestimation, prompting drivers to drive faster than in clear conditions.
evaluation: Claims C53, C56, and C105 are supported by Experiment 2 data showing participants drove faster with uniform reduction (93.6 and 101.3 km/hr) compared to clear visibility (85.1 km/hr). This behavioral pattern is consistent with the perceptual underestimation observed in Experiment 1.

result: Perceived speed depends on the spatial distribution of contrast rather than global contrast level per se, as demonstrated by opposite perceptual effects with identical global contrast reduction.
evaluation: Claims C6, C33, C58, C59, C60, C96, C98, and C99 are strongly supported by the key experimental control showing fog and uniform reduction had identical RMS contrast (0.31 moderate, 0.19 severe) yet produced opposite perceptual effects. This demonstrates that spatial distribution, not just global level, determines perceived speed.

result: The anti-fog manipulation (reversed visibility gradient) produces speed underestimation opposite to natural fog, supporting the hypothesis that relative contrast between central and peripheral visual fields determines perceived speed.
evaluation: Claims C68, C71, C76-C79, C101, and C102 are supported by Experiment 3 data showing anti-fog produced speed underestimation (PSE = 121.6 km/hr matched to 60.1 km/hr clear, equivalent to 19 km/hr perceived) opposite to fog (47.7 km/hr PSE, equivalent to 74.3 km/hr perceived), with statistical significance (p<0.001, ηG2 = 0.81). This confirms the visibility gradient hypothesis.

result: Behavioral driving data with anti-fog confirms the perceptual findings, with drivers driving slower in fog and faster in anti-fog compared to clear visibility.
evaluation: Claims C88, C89, and C90 are supported by Experiment 4 data showing participants drove slower in fog (53.1 km/hr) and faster in anti-fog (104.4 km/hr) compared to clear visibility (67.9 km/hr), with all conditions differing significantly (p<0.05). This validates the perception-behavior link.

result: Speed discrimination sensitivity is reduced for unusual types of contrast reduction (uniform and anti-fog) that are rarely encountered in real life.
evaluation: Claims C45, C46, C82, C83, and C86 are supported by JND data from Experiments 1 and 3 showing higher JNDs (lower sensitivity) for uniform reduction (0.58 km/hr) and anti-fog (0.543 km/hr) compared to clear and fog conditions (0.40-0.42 km/hr and 0.225-0.248 km/hr respectively), with statistical significance.

result: There is a direct relationship between perceived speed and produced driving speed across all experimental conditions.
evaluation: Claims C103 and C106 are supported by the consistent pattern across Experiments 1-4 showing that perceptual biases (overestimation/underestimation) systematically correspond to behavioral responses (slower/faster driving). The parallel results from perception and behavior experiments provide strong converging evidence.

result: Existing theoretical models (Bayesian and ratio models) do not account for the observed differences between uniform and distance-dependent contrast reduction.
evaluation: Claims C137, C138, and C139 are supported by logical analysis showing that existing models address only global contrast effects and cannot explain opposite perceptual biases with identical global contrast but different spatial distributions. This represents a clear limitation of current theoretical frameworks.

result: Reduced discrimination sensitivity for unusual contrast patterns may result from lack of real-world experience with these conditions.
evaluation: Claims C47 and C84 propose a speculative explanation for the observed JND differences. While the pattern is consistent with this hypothesis (unusual conditions show worse discrimination), no direct evidence is provided to test whether ecological frequency determines discrimination performance. This remains an untested hypothesis.

result: Prior work by the authors showed that speed perception depends on which portion of the visual field is visible, with central occlusion causing overestimation and peripheral occlusion causing underestimation.
evaluation: Claims C64, C65, C66, and C67 reference prior published work (Pretto et al., 2009) that established the relationship between visual field occlusion and speed perception. This prior work provides the theoretical foundation for the current fog/anti-fog hypothesis.

result: The experimental design using textured roadsides without landmarks provided robust visual flow information while preventing cognitive biases from potential obstacles.
evaluation: Claims C109, C110, C114-C118 are supported by the experimental design rationale and validation data showing accurate speed estimates (PSE near actual speed) and low JNDs in clear visibility conditions. This demonstrates the stimulus provided sufficient perceptual information for reliable speed judgments.

result: The study employed rigorous psychophysical methods (Bayesian adaptive 2IFC) and immersive virtual reality with careful control of contrast parameters across conditions.
evaluation: Claims C23-C26, C33, C34, C146-C162 describe methodological details that are internally consistent and follow established psychophysical practices. The Bayesian adaptive method, sample sizes (n=10-12 per experiment), and contrast measurements (RMS values) are appropriate for the research questions.

result: Prior research established that speed is underestimated at low contrast, which was proposed as an explanation for excessive driving speed in fog.
evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C9-C11, C93, and C94 accurately represent the consensus from prior literature (Thompson 1982, Snowden et al. 1998, etc.). However, the current study challenges this explanation by showing that the prior work used uniform contrast reduction, which does not accurately model real fog.

result: Previous studies used uniform contrast reduction which is appropriate for 2D stimuli but is a poor model for atmospheric fog in 3D environments.
evaluation: Claims C12-C14, C19-C22 provide accurate critical analysis of prior methodology. The distinction between uniform reduction (appropriate for 2D) and distance-dependent reduction (appropriate for fog) is logically sound and represents a key conceptual contribution identifying a gap in prior research.

result: Neurophysiological findings on contrast-dependent neural activity and theoretical models (Bayesian and ratio models) provide partial but incomplete explanations for contrast effects on speed perception.
evaluation: Claims C119-C136 accurately summarize relevant neurophysiology and theory from cited literature. The discussion appropriately notes both the successes (e.g., Bayesian models predicting underestimation) and limitations (inability to explain opposite effects with same global contrast) of existing frameworks.

result: In fog, better visibility in peripheral regions and impaired visibility in central regions creates a spatial gradient where fog acts as a central mask.
evaluation: Claims C61, C62, and C63 provide logical inference about the spatial distribution of visibility in fog based on physical properties and viewing geometry. This reasoning is sound and supported by citation (Snowden and Freeman 2004), forming the basis for the mechanistic hypothesis.

result: Driving speed variability was twice as large in anti-fog compared to clear and fog conditions.
evaluation: Claim C92 is supported by Experiment 4 data showing variability of 17.6 km/hr in anti-fog versus 9 and 7.5 km/hr in clear and fog conditions. This suggests greater difficulty maintaining consistent speed in the artificial anti-fog condition.

result: Statistical analyses confirm significant effects of visibility conditions on speed perception and driving behavior across all experiments.
evaluation: Claims C35, C36, C41-C43, C54, C57, C75, C80, and C81 report statistical results with appropriate tests (repeated-measures ANOVA), corrections (Huynh-Feldt), and post-hoc comparisons. Effect sizes are large (ηG2 = 0.61-0.81) and p-values highly significant (p<0.001), supporting the robustness of findings.
